data.targetWord: an estate controlled by a lord, including land, buildings, peasants, courts and rights over the local area

examples.en-GB: A typical manor included a manor house, a church, open fields, common land, a mill and peasant cottages.

data.targetWord: a peasant who was legally tied to a manor, owing labour services, rent and other duties to the lord

examples.en-GB: As a villein, Thomas had to work on the lord's land several days a week and could not leave the manor without permission.

data.targetWord: a peasant or townsman with more legal freedom than a villein, able to move more freely, rent land and use different courts

examples.en-GB: Unlike villeins, freemen could take their disputes to royal courts rather than only the manor court.

data.targetWord: a system where each peasant family farmed scattered strips of land in the village open fields

examples.en-GB: Strip farming spread risk because if one part of the field was flooded, a family might still harvest crops from strips in other areas.

data.targetWord: land that villagers had the right to use, for example for grazing animals, collecting wood or gathering resources

examples.en-GB: Poorer villagers depended heavily on common land for grazing their animals and collecting firewood.

data.targetWord: a thick soup or stew made from vegetables, grains and sometimes meat, a staple food for poorer medieval people

examples.en-GB: Most peasant families ate pottage regularly, using vegetables from the garden and grain from the harvest.

data.targetWord: an organisation of craftspeople or merchants in a town that controlled training, standards, prices and membership

examples.en-GB: The bakers' guild set standards for bread quality and punished members who used false weights or sold poor-quality bread.

data.targetWord: a young person living with and training under a skilled master to learn a trade, usually over several years

examples.en-GB: After completing his apprenticeship, John became a journeyman carpenter and worked for wages before applying to become a master.

data.targetWord: a local court dealing with village rules, land transfers, fines and minor offences, which recorded many details of everyday medieval life

examples.en-GB: The manor court record shows a peasant was fined for letting his pigs damage a neighbour's crops.

data.targetWord: a public call for help when a crime was discovered; neighbours were expected to join in chasing the suspect

examples.en-GB: When the thief was spotted leaving the market, a hue and cry was raised and people ran to help catch him.

data.targetWord: a medieval method of determining guilt based on a religious test, such as carrying hot iron, in the belief that God would reveal the truth; it declined after 1215

examples.en-GB: After the Church withdrew support for trial by ordeal in 1215, English courts increasingly relied on juries and investigation.

data.targetWord: a payment, often one tenth of produce or income, made to support the Church

examples.en-GB: Every year, villagers paid a tithe to the local church, giving a tenth of their produce.

data.targetWord: a trader who bought and sold goods, sometimes over long distances; successful merchants could become wealthy and influential in medieval towns

examples.en-GB: Wealthy wool merchants became important figures in English towns, funding churches, guilds and local government.

data.targetWord: duties owed to another person; villeins owed work, payments and restrictions to their lord

examples.en-GB: A villein's obligations included working on the lord's land, paying rent and using only the lord's mill.

data.targetWord: an official who managed a lord's estate, supervised manor business and ran the manor court

examples.en-GB: The steward kept records of rents and obligations, ensuring the lord's estate was run efficiently.

data.targetWord: the deadly pandemic that reached England in 1348-1349, killing a large proportion of the population and causing lasting changes to labour relations and society

examples.en-GB: After the Black Death reduced the population sharply, surviving labourers could sometimes demand higher wages because workers were scarce.

data.targetWord: the uprising of 1381 in which ordinary people protested against taxation, labour laws and social hierarchy, marching on London before being suppressed

examples.en-GB: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 showed that ordinary people could challenge the government, even though the uprising was ultimately suppressed.

data.targetWord: systems for keeping places clean and healthy, especially regarding the removal of human waste and rubbish; medieval towns had limited sanitation

examples.en-GB: Poor sanitation in medieval towns, with waste in streets and polluted water, helped diseases spread rapidly.

data.targetWord: disease among livestock, which could devastate a village's farming capacity and cause serious hardship

examples.en-GB: Murrain killed many cattle in the village that year, leaving families without animals to plough the fields.

data.targetWord: a group of ten households that were collectively responsible for each other's behaviour in the local law system

examples.en-GB: If a member of a tithing committed a crime and escaped, the other members of the group could be fined.

data.targetWord: a detailed list of a person's possessions, often made after death; inventories help historians understand how ordinary medieval people lived

examples.en-GB: The inventory taken after the peasant's death listed a wooden chest, two pots, a bed and tools worth a few shillings.

data.targetWord: the period of harvest failures and food shortages from 1315 to 1317 that caused widespread hunger and hardship across England and Europe

examples.en-GB: The Great Famine of 1315-1317 showed how dependent medieval people were on good harvests for their survival.

data.targetWord: large village fields divided into strips farmed by different families, a common farming system in medieval England

examples.en-GB: The village open fields were divided into strips so that each family had land in different areas, spreading the risk of poor harvests.

data.targetWord: the forced removal of a group from a place; Edward I expelled Jewish people from England in 1290

examples.en-GB: The expulsion of Jewish people from England in 1290 was an act of royal persecution that ended centuries of Jewish community life.

data.targetWord: a survey of land, resources and people ordered by William I in 1086, providing historians with detailed information about post-Conquest England

examples.en-GB: Historians use the Domesday Book to understand who owned land in England shortly after the Norman Conquest.

data.title: Arrange the stages of a medieval apprenticeship career in order
items: Family agrees for child to enter service with a master
Apprentice lives with master and learns the trade
Apprentice completes training and becomes a journeyman
Journeyman works for wages for another master
Journeyman creates a 'masterpiece' and applies to join the guild
Master operates own workshop and trains new apprentices
